headline: This law lets injured federal first responders keep their early-retirement benefits even after moving to a regular civil service job.
what_it_does: Federal first responders such as law enforcement officers, customs and border protection officers, and firefighters usually must retire at age 57 and pay a higher share of salary toward retirement. This law lets a disabled first responder keep these benefits as if they had not been disabled. If an injured first responder is moved to a civil service job outside the first responder system after returning from a work injury or illness, they can stay in that system. If they leave federal service before they can collect an annuity, they may get a refund of their higher retirement contributions.

who_it_affects.how: Officers who are disabled by a work-related injury or illness can keep their early-retirement benefits and the accelerated retirement system if they return to a different civil service job.
Firefighters who are disabled on the job can keep their accelerated retirement benefits and may get a refund of extra contributions if they leave service before receiving an annuity.

Officers injured on the job can stay in the accelerated retirement system after moving to a non-first-responder federal job, and may get a refund of extra contributions if they leave before receiving an annuity.

when_it_takes_effect: The law was enacted on December 9, 2022. The official summary does not list any later effective dates.
